system.name: JENGA
system.one_liner: A memory allocation framework that manages heterogeneous KV-cache embeddings in LLM serving via a two-level allocator and layer-specific caching APIs.

content.subject: comparing imbalanced, unaligned, and balanced-aligned KV-cache eviction policies across two heterogeneous layer types

panels.label: (a) imbalanced (only evict sliding window)
panels.differs: only the sliding-window layer's cache is evicted, so both its tokens are blank while self-attention keeps Hello and World

panels.label: (b) unaligned (evicted tokens are different)
panels.differs: each layer evicts one token but a different one (self-attention evicts World, window evicts Hello), so no complete prefix survives in all layers

panels.label: (c) balanced & aligned
panels.differs: both layers evict the same token, World, in equal number, leaving Hello present and aligned across every layer

content.key_idea: Only evicting the same tokens in balanced numbers across both layer types keeps their caches aligned, so a later request can still hit; imbalanced or unaligned eviction breaks the hit.
content.reading_order: Left to right from the shared current cache, then top to bottom through branches (a), (b), (c) to each outcome icon.

style.stroke: black ~1pt grid/arrow lines; warm gold-brown (#bc8c00) borders on filled orange/yellow cells; green (#507e32) border on the happy-face icon
style.arrows: solid black arrowheads on straight connecting lines, one per branch label and one from the new-request box to each outcome
style.icons: hand-drawn circular face glyphs: amber frowning faces for the two No-hit outcomes, one green smiling face for the Hit outcome

encoding.color_means: warm orange/yellow shades identify which layer type a cache cell belongs to (self-attention vs sliding-window); grey marks an evicted/empty cell; amber vs green marks a failed vs successful cache lookup
encoding.line_style_means: plain solid arrows connect the starting cache to each alternative's resulting cache and outcome; no dashed lines are used
encoding.state_means: before/after eviction is told apart by cell fill: a filled, coloured cell still holds its token, a blank grey cell has been evicted
encoding.marker_means: letters (a)/(b)/(c) identify the three eviction strategies compared; face icons and 'Hit'/'No hit' text mark the resulting verdict
encoding.emphasis: only the bottom (c) branch ends in a green smiling face and an explicit 'Hit: Hello', visually singling out the balanced-and-aligned policy as the one that works
reusable_patterns: one shared starting state fanning out into lettered alternative branches, each ending in a pass/fail face icon
weaknesses: the 'Hello' and 'World' cell labels repeat across rows and panels, so the semantic record cannot key each surviving/evicted cell by name alone; row and column position disambiguate instead

evidence: Balanced and aligned cache eviction policy can improve hit rate.
It is important to balance the number of evicted tokens across different layer types.
Eviction policies across layers must be aligned to ensure that similar sets of tokens are evicted.

summary: This single tikz drawing compares three cache-eviction strategies for LLM serving with heterogeneous layer types. Starting from one shared cache holding Hello and World tokens in both a self-attention row and a sliding-window row, three lettered branches show what happens when two pages must be evicted. In (a), only the window layer is evicted, leaving the layers imbalanced; in (b), each layer evicts a different token, leaving them unaligned; in (c), both layers evict the same token, World, keeping them balanced and aligned. A new request for 'Hello World' is then checked against each resulting cache: (a) and (b) both miss, shown with amber frowning faces and 'No hit', while only the balanced-and-aligned (c) branch hits, shown with a green smiling face and 'Hit: Hello'.
